Chapter 2. Into the Ice—Hope, Uncertainty, and the First Trials.
In those first days aboard the Jeannette, you could feel the sense of purpose pulsing through the ship. Men from all kinds of backgrounds came together, united by that one big dream—reaching the Pole. Life on the ship quickly found its rhythm: standing watch, checking equipment, sharing meals. At first, the Arctic almost seemed to welcome them. The sun just hovered on the horizon, casting this unreal, never-ending twilight across the ice.
But as the Jeannette pushed further north, the crew started to see the Arctic for what it really was—a living, shifting force. The ice wasn’t just some frozen wall. It groaned, it cracked, sometimes opening a path one moment, then snapping it shut the next. Each day, moving forward got harder. Frustration crept in—maybe when a channel that looked promising suddenly froze over, or when the bitter cold seemed to seep into every last inch of the ship.
De Long’s leadership was tested right from the start. He ran a tight ship, insisting on discipline and routine, but he also knew how important it was to keep everyone’s spirits up. He encouraged the men to write in their journals, play games, and look for those little comforts that make a world of difference during tough times. Sure, there were moments of tension—different personalities and the strain of living in such close quarters—but for the most part, the crew adapted. They learned to respect the ice, to watch for subtle changes, and above all, to trust one another.
The expedition’s scientists stayed busy, too—measuring, collecting samples, and trying to make sense of this strange, frozen world. Every observation felt important, like they were part of something bigger than themselves. The dream of finding an Open Polar Sea still flickered in their minds, but it was clear now—the Arctic was far more complex, and way more dangerous, than anyone had guessed.
Weeks slipped by, then months, and the Jeannette found herself locked in the ice. At first, hope lingered—a shift in the wind, or a change in the current, might set them free. But the ice wasn’t letting go. The ship became a prisoner, drifting wherever the frozen sea decided to take her. The crew adjusted to a new routine: fixing what they could, rationing supplies, and waiting for any sign of escape.
Most people never realize how quickly hope can turn to anxiety in a place like that. The endless daylight faded into darkness, and the cold grew sharper. The sense of isolation pressed down, making it clear that the Arctic had its own rules—and didn’t care about anyone’s plans. Yet, even with all that uncertainty, the men held on to a stubborn determination. They refused to give up. No matter how long it took, they were going to find a way forward.
